findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify and prove the write-fence enforcement mechanism (how the auto-push remote is quiesced and in-flight pushes drained over an unregistered, continuously-pushing clone set with no clone registry), or downgrade the <N-day 'zero observable loss' claim to a bounded-risk statement consistent with the no-registry model.
evidence: Plan: 'the sync remote is quiesced and all in-flight pushes are drained before the swap — so no live (<N-day) clone holds unpushed divergent writes at swap time'
DESIGN comment concedes: 'P2 needs a maintenance window, non-trivial for a continuously-pushing store'
536b escalation: 'The tracker has no registry of clones and no observed-compaction watermark'
ABSENCE: no mechanism given for how pushes from unregistered clients are actually blocked/drained during the window
findings.finding: The write-fence ('quiesce the sync remote and drain all in-flight pushes before the swap') is the load-bearing mechanism that makes the <N-day-clone loss zero, but the plan asserts it without specifying HOW it is enforced against a distributed, unregistered, ~14K-writes/day auto-pushing clone set. The epic's own founding premise is that the tracker has 'no registry of clones' (536b escalation comments); a global write-fence over clients you cannot enumerate is not obviously achievable, and the DESIGN comment itself concedes the fence is 'non-trivial for a continuously-pushing store'.
findings.location: Plan section 'Swap safety for ALL clone states (extends C3)' and AC 'C1–C5 proven to prevent resurrection across all clone states, incl. a <N-day clone with unpushed writes'
scenarios: A live <N-day clone pushes an unpushed divergent write during or just after the fence window because there is no enforceable global quiesce, and that write is lost — contradicting the 'loses NO observable work' claim.
The proof's zero-loss guarantee for <N-day clones rests on an assumption that cannot be discharged in the current no-registry model.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] In §S2, name the concrete git history-rewrite primitive the coalescing builds on (e.g. git filter-repo / git replace+graft / git fast-import) and record its evidence class — confirm it is present in the disposable-clone/out-of-band environment and that it reduces reachable objects on the PUSHED ref (grafts/replace are local-only), routing to a SPIKE if unconfirmed.
evidence: Plan: 'S2 history coalescing to a re-signed baseline checkpoint ... Broadened from `.retired`-only to commit/tree reclamation (the object-count lever).'
Plan: 'Mechanism (portable, out-of-band; NO CI-provider dependence)'
repo search: `git filter-repo` has ZERO references in src/ or infra/ (only a prior plan-review cache entry) — UNVERIFIED whether the tool is installed/available in the disposable-clone environment
The internal verbs it composes with (`rebar fsck`, `rebar verify-authorship`, `authorship_ledger`, `identity.enforce_since`) DO exist and are already used — those are not new integrations.
findings.finding: S2's history-coalescing / commit-tree reclamation mechanism depends on a git history-rewrite primitive that is never named, and whose availability in the 'disposable clone' environment is unverified. `git filter-repo` (the natural candidate) is not vendored or referenced anywhere in the repo. The plan calls the mechanism 'portable' and 'out-of-band' and describes 'the swap is one revertible ref update', but without naming the primitive (filter-repo vs replace+graft vs fast-import vs shallow-graft) the portability/feasibility claim is unverifiable.
findings.location: Mechanism §S2 + Acceptance Criteria 'Safe mechanism S0-S3 designed (portable, out-of-band)'
scenarios: S2 shadow-clone prototype (deferred slice) reaches for `git filter-repo` on a runner where it is not installed → mechanism is not portable as claimed
A replace/graft-based approach is chosen instead but does not actually reduce reachable object count on push (grafts are local-only) → the pack-shrink win does not materialize
findings.suggested_fix: State the primitive explicitly and probe it: e.g. 'S2 uses `git filter-repo --commit-callback` (or `git fast-export | git fast-import`) in the disposable clone; git-filter-repo is not a rebar dependency today, so S1 includes a capability probe / SPIKE confirming the tool is installed and that the rewritten shadow ref, when fetched blobless, drops the object count as modeled.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the post-rollback state assertion: after reverting origin/tickets to the backup ref, define how already-force-reset clones (C3) are reconciled back, confirm no residual mixed-baseline divergence, and attach a `DATA LOSS RISK` note for any clone/divergent work not recoverable by the revert.
evidence: Plan: 'Rollback: immutable backup ref refs/tickets-backup/pre-reclaim-<date> before the swap; ... the swap is one revertible ref update'

Applicability: this is an in-place rewrite / one-way transformation of persisted records (every commit SHA changes) AND C3 forces stale/live clones to reset to remote — clients are mutated as part of the migration, so reverting the shared ref does not un-reset already-reset clones

ABSENCE: the plan does not state what a post-revert reconcile does to clones that already force-reset to the collapsed baseline, nor confirm no residual mixed-baseline / observable-state divergence after rollback
findings.finding: The rollback design asserts the ref swap is revertible (revert origin/tickets to the backup ref) but does not assert on the CLONE-POPULATION STATE after that revert: clones already force-reset to the collapsed baseline via C3 during the swap window, and >N-day divergent work already discarded, are not shown to be recoverable by reverting the shared ref. A revert can 'complete' while leaving a mixed/incorrectly-baselined clone population.
findings.location: Risk / rollback section ('the swap is one revertible ref update; never prune the backup until a green ... run + full reconcile') and C3 forced-override
scenarios: Swap lands; several live clones auto-fetch and force-reset to the new collapsed baseline; a defect is found and the ref is reverted to the backup — those clones now sit on an abandoned baseline while origin holds the old SHAs
A green Verify Authorship Identity run is treated as the rollback success signal, but the 'full reconcile' step that must restore clone state is undefined
findings.suggested_fix: Extend the rollback section to (1) define the 'full reconcile' step's effect on clone state after a revert (e.g., clones re-fetch and reset back to the reverted backup baseline), (2) assert the post-revert observable ticket state equals pre-swap state on both origin and reconciled clones, verified by fsck/replay/verify-authorship, and (3) explicitly label as DATA LOSS RISK any >N-day divergent work that cannot be recovered even after rollback.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Prove the coalescing baseline preserves positionally-stray in-horizon events (the ADR 0035 rebuild-on-stray / SNAPSHOT_INCONSISTENT class), showing how a concurrent sub-horizon event that sorts before a folded SNAPSHOT survives collapse of pre-horizon history.
evidence: Plan: 'those events are above the horizon and untouched by the collapse of pre-horizon history'

ADR 0035: 'A concurrent event authored on the other clone … can, after a merge-as-union reconvergence, land in the ticket directory sorting before the snapshot' — dropped by positional skip unless handled by rebuild-on-stray
concurrency.md:57-59: a reversed-to-active source 'sorts before the SNAPSHOT and is positionally skipped during replay'
findings.finding: The mechanism claims a <N-day clone 'replays its post-baseline (in-horizon) events onto the new baseline (those events are above the horizon and untouched by the collapse of pre-horizon history)', but ADR 0035 establishes that under merge-as-union a concurrent sub-horizon event authored on another clone can land sorting BEFORE a snapshot and is handled only by rebuild-on-stray. The proof does not show these positionally-interleaving in-horizon/stray events survive collapse of pre-horizon history into one checkpoint.
findings.location: Plan section 'Swap safety for ALL clone states'; DESIGN comment P2 coalesce step
scenarios: A concurrent sub-horizon sibling event that merged in after a horizon-aged SNAPSHOT was cut sorts before that snapshot; when history is collapsed to a single baseline checkpoint, it is neither folded (absent from source_event_uuids) nor preserved as a live post-baseline event — silent loss of an observable event.
fsck/replay on the shadow branch passes only because the stray event was already reconciled, masking the coalescing gap on a live store where a stray is mid-reconvergence.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an explicit approach-ordering rationale weighing 'W1/W2 prevention first + re-measure' against 'history rewrite first', and justify why the destructive coalescing is worth its blast radius given the plan's own finding that W1/W2 are the durable root-cause fix.
evidence: Plan: 'History GC is symptomatic; the disease is per-event commit granularity + full-width root-tree churn'
Plan: W1 'Biggest durable lever'; even a rewrite 're-crosses 481 MiB in ~4 days' at ~28 MiB/day
Plan: the rewrite is 'a non-FF force-update of a shared, auto-pushed, high-write-rate branch' — the largest blast radius available
ABSENCE: no comparison of a W1/W2-first sequencing against the rewrite-first sequencing
findings.finding: The plan sequences the highest-blast-radius action (a full history rewrite / non-FF force-update of a shared auto-pushed branch) as the primary lever, while deferring W1 (enrichment/digest write-batching) and W2 (root-tree sharding) as out-of-scope follow-ups — even though the plan's own analysis names those as 'the biggest durable lever' and 'the disease', and calls the rewrite 'symptomatic'. A reviewer-generated alternative (land W1/W2 prevention first, re-measure, then decide whether a destructive rewrite is still warranted) is plausibly superior on blast-radius and may shrink or eliminate the rewrite; the plan does not weigh this ordering.
findings.location: Plan sections 'Quantified win — insufficient alone' and 'Mechanism'; DESIGN comment recommendation 2–3
scenarios: The destructive rewrite is executed (after approval) but growth resumes at ~14K commits/day, re-breaching within days, so the high-risk one-shot buys little durable value that W1/W2 would not have bought at far lower risk.
W1/W2 alone, plus the W3 bridge, could keep the gate green without ever needing a shared-branch history rewrite — an option the plan never evaluates.
findings.suggested_fix: In the DESIGN, evaluate landing W1 (write-batching) and W2 (root-tree sharding) with the W3 budget bridge FIRST, re-measure the blobless pack growth rate, and only then decide whether the shared-branch history rewrite is still required — stating why the chosen ordering is at-least-as-good on blast-radius and durability.
